one of the most requested features across both the runners and community repositories. Letting you define configuration settings once with an anchor (&) and reference them elsewhere with an alias (*).

we released non-public workflow templates, a longstanding request from organizations that want consistent, private workflow scaffolding. Non-public workflow templates let organizations set up common templates for their teams directly in their .github repository.

When a job is skipped because it’s if condition is not met, it’s very difficult to debug why that happened. It would be valuable to be able to see debug logs for the evaluation of the job-level if condition.
It’s sometimes possible to work around this by creating another job without a conditional and then creating steps with the same if condition that is used at the job-level for another job (Example). title: Support --ignore-revs-file for blame view to support automated code formatters
query:
Support --ignore-revs-file for blame view to support automated code formatters
When using automated code formatters to format a legacy project (read: code not matching an automated code formatter's style) it would be splendid to be able to make sure the commits related to the reformatting wouldn't be taken into account in GitHub's blame page.
Here's some background in the docs for Python's popular "black" code formatter: 
A long-standing argument against moving to automated code formatters like Black is that the migration will clutter up the output of git blame. This was a valid argument, but since Git version 2.23, Git natively supports ignoring revisions in blame with the --ignore-rev option. You can also pass a file listing the revisions to ignore using the --ignore-revs-file option. The changes made by the revision will be ignored when assigning blame. Lines modified by an ignored revision will be blamed on the previous revision that modified those lines.
In case anyone wants to spread the call for this feature in their network, feel free to retweet 🥳

title: [projects beta] Handling features within a project (epics/umbrellas)
query:
[projects beta] Handling features within a project (epics/umbrellas)
I just started using the new projects beta and try to get my things organized in a way I am familiar with. Not sure if I am using it the right way but I will try to share some insights into my work style and hope it helps understanding the things which I am struggling with 😁:
In my environment each project is a release cycle. So I create one project for each release I plan (e.g. MyProject 1.3). Now with the project created the project planning starts: I need to think of the features I want to deliver within this release cycle. I do this by adding draft items to the project. Then I convert the features into issues in the repos and describe them. There I create then the feature breakdown using task lists and let GH create another sub-issue for each task. In each sub-issue I then describe again what is addressed there and maybe I already add sub-tasks what I have to take care of there. An example:
In MyProject 1.3 I add native Android support in my cross platform library. As a first sub-issue I extend my toolchain to build a native Android library. The second sub-issue is about adding a proper android control for usage in projects. And the third sub-issue is about creating a deploy chain to package managers like maven for others to consume. Each sub-issue has again subtasks like extending the codebase, tests, documentation,.. that have to be covered.
This project style is coming more from the scrum work style with a epic > stories > subtask structure where epics are usually larger features, stories are the broken down parts which fit into sprints and subtasks is the split of the work within the team (implementation, documentation, testing,..). Thinking of other (scrum) issue tracking systems I got in tough with, this structure was always somehow possible (CA Agile, Jira) and it seems especially large repositories on GH practice similar work styles where large scale features need to be broken down with a clean planning phase of a new project release cycle.
Problem 1: Issue structure
GitHub does not directly have the concept of nested issues where a parent can be considered an epic/feature. You can try to do it by creating issues where you link the other issues with task lists. This is nicely described here: But this does not integrate well with the new projects beta yet. 😞
With the workflow described above you end up with following problems:
The sub-issues are not added of the project by default. You have to add them manually to the project in which the parent issue is already.
The project does not indicate any hierarchy of features > tasks and their progress like it would be the case with a milestone. This progress can only be seen when opening the parent issue where you see a progress indicator on top.
The project board does not allow grouping the issues by their feature > task hierarchy. You just see a flat list of all issues.
Creating automations based on this structure is not easy because there is not a 100% clear semantic about parent > children relationships which is understood by the workflows.
Workarounds
You can try to workaround this a bit by naming conventions and manual sorting to make it look like a nested hierarchy but it is not really intuitive this way.
You can use milestones as features instead of umbrella/parent issues. You see the tracking on milestone level and also the board allows grouping by milestone. But it does not seem to be the intended way of milestones, because you can not track "real" project milestones like a 1.3 feature complete anymore.
Problem 2: Board persistence
You cannot define a board to have a default layout for everyone who opens it. I would like to create boards with defined filters and grouping rules that cannot be changed (only extended?). With this feature mentality I would like to have boards like the following in my project:
Release status
Here you see only "feature" issues (aka. umbrella issues or epic issues) and their accumulated status. You see the X/Y subtasks progress the general status. It is like a high level release progress view what is still to be done until the release/end-of-project without going into the details what each feature still needs.
Feature status
In this view you see the "Feature > Sub-Issue" levels in a grouping mode. For each feature you can inspect what sub-issues/parts are required to complete the feature. It allows more detailed tracking on where each feature stands.
Workarounds
As mentioned above, maybe with milestones you can get the desired grouping.
You can keep "draft items" as groups and just sort the items into the sections.
Solution proposals
While I am not sure if my work style fits the one of others too, I see the need for the following topics somehow addressed in the new projects system somehow:
It would be good to make the parent > children relationship (the one with task lists) a first class citizen in the new projects beta to really allow a feature level view to the project you're working on. It should be clearly documented and described how you can achieve a feature > feature-part > sub-task structure within the issues and projects can be organized. Maybe even deeper structures are required by some people.
This nesting also needs to be supported in the workflows. e.g. a feature gets put into progress if any child issue is put into progress. A issue gets put into progress when you create a PR referencing it. Otherwise you end up setting all status values manually while you want to focus on executing your planned project work.
It should be possible to define a base filtering/sorting/grouping for each board which is persisted and applied to everyone. Users might add additional filtering or sorting on top to filter the base view.
There is a need for a column in boards that indicate the progress of this issue respecting the subtasks (e.g. a progress bar showing X/Y tasks completed).
Overall it would be great to have some reference examp
